Adult Sulphur goatfish (Upeneus sulphureus) in the Gulf of Thailand typically attain a maximum fork length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], a value derived from extensive trawl surveys across the demersal fishing grounds. This ultimate size places the species among the medium-bodied members of the Mullidae, with asymptotic body mass reaching approximately 174.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 174.3 grams] based on length-weight regressions calculated from landed catch samples. The largest individuals are consistently recorded from deeper, less-fished strata, suggesting that fishing pressure may truncate the upper end of the size distribution in more accessible coastal waters.

Sexual maturation in this species initiates at a relatively modest size, with the fork length at puberty documented at 9.9 centimeters [Lp = 9.9 centimeters]. This threshold marks the point at which gonadal recrudescence becomes evident during histological examination of the ovaries, typically observed in individuals between six and eight months of age. The onset of reproductive activity at this fork length is consistent with the pattern seen in other tropical mullids, where early maturation is favored under conditions of elevated natural mortality. The ability to begin spawning at a fork length of less than ten centimeters represents a significant life-history adaptation to the warm, resource-variable environment of the Indo-West Pacific.

Reproductive output under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] has been estimated from comparative data across congeners. Field studies indicate that females produce approximately one clutch every three to four days during the peak spawning season, with each spawning event yielding several hundred oocytes [N_R_i = each spawning event yielding several hundred oocytes], and the frequency of these events sustaining a high daily fecundity. The maximum reproductive rate, assessed at this temperature, is estimated at 262.5 eggs per day [Ri = 262.5 eggs per day] for a fully mature female at the upper end of the size range. This elevated output is facilitated by the continuous batch-spawning strategy typical of the genus Upeneus, which allows for the rapid turnover of oocyte cohorts under consistently warm conditions.

At the onset of independent life, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a minimal endogenous nutrient reserve, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00062 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00062 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter documented for this species. The pelagic, transparent eggs measure roughly one millimeter in diameter, and upon eclosion, the prolarva relies entirely on its yolk sac for sustenance prior to the commencement of exogenous feeding. This initial mass is among the lowest recorded for commercially exploited goatfishes in the region, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over large offspring size. The lecithotrophic phase is brief, typically lasting no more than two to three days at local ambient temperatures, after which the larvae must successfully transition to feeding on small planktonic copepods.

Longevity records from tag-recapture studies and otolith ageing place the maximum lifespan of Upeneus sulphureus at 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is characteristic of small, fast-growing tropical demersal fishes that experience high rates of natural predation. The age structure of wild populations is heavily skewed toward younger year classes, with very few individuals persisting beyond their third year. The trade-off between rapid maturation and brief longevity is evident: early puberty at a fork length of just 9.9 centimeters [Lp = 9.9 centimeters] allows the species to compensate for its abbreviated adult phase by channeling substantial energy into continuous reproductive effort throughout the warm monsoon seasons.
